name: Gareth Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. What you tell me is confidential; could you describe a usual shift building or repairing power lines?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a crew for the electricity company, and most mornings begin with permits, a truck check and somebody reminding the new lad to test twice. My two-year technical diploma matters, but so does knowing which old spans whip in the wind.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What keeps you in the job, and what is hard about it now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like a clean repair and a crew that gets home whole. At forty-three I still climb, then go home to my partner Mina, our two schoolchildren and a mortgage; we have a few months saved, so I watch the overtime list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew a bit of paperwork done by AI will not change what a live conductor can do. I have never used an AI tool and would rather keep my hand-written check list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I’d be glad if jobs and pay stayed much as they are. Typical pay covers our mortgage and we have a few months put by, though the children’s costs seem to grow every term.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep leading the crew and checking the paper permit against the line at the site. This year I’d keep our monthly family budget on the fridge and leave the existing savings available for a real emergency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about my work in that picture, with the ordinary worry of keeping the household budget straight. A quiet year would suit us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the first mark on your check list?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I mark that two people have read the isolation number aloud and tested the line. A tidy AI form cannot replace two lineworkers reading the isolation number aloud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the fridge budget tell Mina and the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Mina can see how much is left after the mortgage and school costs each month. The children see why we sometimes choose a park afternoon over a ticketed outing.

say: **Paper permits** and spoken isolation checks still govern my line crew.
Small **AI paperwork** savings would not change the physical repair job.
think: Our **few months saved** and typical pay make the mortgage manageable if hours hold.
The growing **school costs** remain a household pressure.
do: **Keep** leading repairs and reading isolation numbers aloud before testing.
**Keep** a monthly family budget visible on the fridge.
feel: **Calm** about steady work, while still minding ordinary family costs.
S0.quote: A tidy AI form cannot replace two lineworkers reading the isolation number aloud.
fieldNote: Gareth has never used **AI tools** and relies on a spoken two-person check at each isolation.
He keeps existing **savings** available, which is not counted as new saving.

steps.text: Keep reading isolation numbers aloud before each line test
Keep the monthly household budget on the fridge

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say the office can try software for buying and planning, but the line crew has to verify the parts and site. I would ask to see a proven ticket beside a real pole before the company changes our routine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I worry faster dispatch will mean another call late in the day without another crew member. Our savings would absorb a short problem, but I do not want to spend them because a program set a foolish timetable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask my supervisor to walk through three new tickets at an actual site before rollout. I’d keep a paper list of missing parts for the first year and send it back whenever the ticket is wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the office moving faster than the field. I can work with a new form once somebody shows it is dependable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which missing part would stop your crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A missing insulating sleeve would stop our line repair before we climb. I would write the pole number and the part on the list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who gets the paper list?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would hand the list to the supervisor who signs our job sheets. If it keeps happening, I would ask that supervisor to bring dispatch to a site.

say: **Planning** and buying may move to software before physical line repair does.
I would require **site checks** before adopting new tickets.
think: Faster **dispatch** could mean late calls and pressure on a small crew.
Our **savings** can cover a short problem, but repeated bad schedules would waste them.
do: **Request** three ticket checks at real poles before rollout.
**Record** missing parts on paper and send wrong tickets to the supervisor.
feel: **Uneasy** about new pace, yet open to a proven form.
S1.quote: A missing insulating sleeve would stop our line repair before we climb.
fieldNote: He will consider change after a **field demonstration**, consistent with his preference for familiar routines.
His **paper list** is a way to correct dispatch errors without claiming new AI skills.

steps.text: Request three ticket checks at actual poles before rollout
Record missing parts on paper for the supervisor

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew thinking AI by 2028 may take over the office, but hands still repair lines until capable robots arrive around 2031. I would want our company to say plainly how many crew posts remain after its robot trials.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I can see a robot taking some of our pole work, and I am not keen to operate one on a live line. We have a few months saved and some other line jobs nearby, but losing my typical wage would still put the mortgage under pressure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the manager for a written crew plan and safety trial dates now. I’d stop booking paid weekend outings for the next year and ask nearby electricity companies about lead openings only if our employer announces actual cuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because the risk to my wage is real, though I still have time to act. I would rather make one careful lineworker job move than chase every robot rumour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children about the outings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell our two children we will do free days by the river while we wait for clearer news about work. I would not tell them the mortgage is their problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you call another electricity company?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would call if our manager gives a real notice that line crews are being cut. Then I would ask the other company about pay, travel and whether a lead vacancy actually exists.

say: **2028 thinking AI** reaches the office before capable line robots around 2031.
I would ask for a written **crew plan** after robot trials.
think: A lost **lineworker wage** would strain the mortgage, even with a few months saved.
I would approach **nearby employers** only after a real cut announcement.
do: **Request** a written crew plan and robot trial dates from the manager.
**Stop** paid weekend outings for the next year.
**Ask** nearby companies about lead vacancies if actual crew cuts are announced.
feel: **Anxious** about wage risk, while still able to act carefully.
S2.quote: I would rather make one careful lineworker job move than chase every robot rumour.
fieldNote: His **job search** has a clear trigger: an actual cut announcement rather than rumours.
He does not claim the **robot** is ready in 2028; its hands-on capability follows around 2031.

steps.text: Stop paid weekend outings for the next year
Ask nearby companies about lead vacancies if cuts are announced

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say thinking AI in 2031 and capable robots around 2034 give us time to test equipment properly. I would ask our safety lead to show the crew a robot working on a dead training line before anybody signs up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I hope the company will still want experienced leads to check what machines build. I could learn a new inspection routine if it is proven and paid, but I would not leave a steady line job for a promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the safety lead for the training-line demonstration schedule this year. After seeing a sound trial, I’d ask about a paid inspection course and enroll only if the company offers a real role that covers our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy rather than rushed. Five years lets me wait for evidence without pretending the household has no bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you watch during the training-line trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would watch how the robot detects a loose connector and whether it stops when a joint differs from the plan. Our crew should see the robot failure procedure, not only a successful lift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the inspection course is unpaid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stay leading repairs and leave the course alone. A few months of savings are for a broken boiler or lost work, not an unpaid bet.

say: **2031 thinking AI** precedes capable line robots around 2034.
A **dead-line trial** should prove the robot can stop at an unexpected fault.
think: Experienced **crew leads** may still check repairs, though no job is promised.
An **unpaid course** would be too risky for our mortgage.
do: **Request** the dead-line robot demonstration schedule from the safety lead.
**Consider** a paid inspection course only after a sound trial and real job offer.
feel: **Uneasy**, but able to wait for evidence while keeping wages.
S3.quote: Our crew should see the robot failure procedure, not only a successful lift.
fieldNote: He wants a **failure procedure** shown in the trial, not just a polished successful lift.
His potential **training** has firm conditions: proven trial, paid course and a post covering the mortgage.

steps.text: Request the dead-line robot demonstration schedule
Consider paid inspection training only after proof and a suitable offer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew thinking AI in 2036 and capable robots around 2039 give us nearly a decade to write proper work rules. We should keep old repair records so any machine can be judged against what crews actually found.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be in my fifties by the time robots reach the poles, and fewer climbing days could be useful. But our mortgage still needs wages, and I would not bring retirement forward just because a machine looks impressive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I’d sort our paper repair notes by fault type and put the worst recurring faults into the annual safety review. I’d keep leading the crew and ask whether a paid inspection role exists when the company has tested the equipment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the long timetable, although the family budget still matters. There is time to decide if a proven inspection job beats the one I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which fault goes to the safety review first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would bring a photograph and the paper note for a corroded joint hidden under a cover. A neat route plan can miss a corroded joint hidden under a cover.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you switch to a screen-based inspection job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would consider it only after seeing the work, hours and pay in a real offer. I have no wish to sit at a screen for less money than this crew earns.

say: **2036 thinking AI** and robots around 2039 leave years to compare machines with past repairs.
I would bring **recurring faults** to the annual safety review.
think: Fewer **climbing days** might suit me in my fifties if inspection work is real.
Our **mortgage** still needs wages; I would not retire early on a guess.
do: **Sort** paper repair notes by fault type this year.
**Bring** recurring faults to the annual crew safety review.
**Ask** about paid inspection roles after company equipment tests.
feel: **Calm** about the long timeline, while still attentive to family costs.
S4.quote: A neat route plan can miss a corroded joint hidden under a cover.
fieldNote: His long-horizon plan begins with **paper records** and a safety review, not sudden adoption of AI.
An inspection move depends on a **tested role** with acceptable hours and pay.

steps.text: Sort paper repair notes by fault type
Bring recurring faults to the crew safety review
Ask about paid inspection roles after equipment tests

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the office could change quickly and robots could put crew wages at risk by 2031. A written staffing plan, a field trial that shows failures, and a real paid inspection offer would help me judge the next step.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask how a crew is meant to refuse a robot job when the pole in front of them does not match the screen. I have seen enough good drawings of bad poles to demand written robot stop-work rules.

headlineQuote: I have seen enough good drawings of bad poles to demand written robot stop-work rules.
portrait: Gareth is a skilled **line crew lead** with a technical diploma, typical pay, a mortgage and a few months saved.
He has never used **AI tools** and relies on spoken isolation checks and paper repair notes.
His centre outlook and resistant style lead to **field proof** before changing tickets, tools or jobs.
Fast AGI makes his **wages uncertain**; more time lets him seek tested, paid inspection work without retiring early.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could change dispatch quickly and put crew wages at risk once robots arrive around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: A written **staffing plan**, honest field trial and paid inspection offer would help him judge the next step.
